quizzes.title: The Three Bills: Who Tabled and What They Cover
quizzes.passage: The 130th Constitution Amendment Bill is part of a package of Bills that deal with removing leaders from office. Together, the Bills propose the removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers under certain conditions. The package reaches several levels of government, including the Union, the states and Delhi, so its rules are not limited to one office. The Bills set out the conditions for removal and name the authority that would act for each office. They also address whether a removed minister may later return to office after release. The Bills were presented as a set, and each one covers a different part of the framework. Each Bill has its own formal name, which the booklet lists in full. A committee is currently examining the main Bill, so the Bills remain under consideration. The rules differ between offices, so the scope of each one depends on the office involved. The booklet presents the conditions in a table that lists the offence threshold, the removal authority for each office and any additional provision. Comparing the rows of that table shows how the rules differ between the Union and the states. These details form the core of the proposal that the booklet describes.

questions.q: Who tabled the three Bills?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the three Bills were tabled by the Home Minister.

questions.q: Which of the three Bills is the Government of Union Territories (Amendment) Bill, 2025?
questions.explanation: The booklet numbers the Government of Union Territories (Amendment) Bill, 2025 as the second Bill.

questions.q: Which body is examining the 130th Constitution Amendment Bill?
options: Standing Committee on Law and Justice
questions.explanation: The booklet says the Joint Parliamentary Committee is examining the Bill.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The 130th Constitution Amendment Bill was introduced in 2025.
Reason (R): The Bill is one of three Bills tabled together.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the tabling of three Bills does not explain the year of introduction.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Article 75   ->   A. Union Ministers
II. Article 164   ->   B. State Ministers and Chief Ministers
III. Article 239AA   ->   C. Chief Minister and Ministers of Delhi
IV. Government of Union Territories Act, 1963   ->   D. Ministers of Union Territories
questions.explanation: Article 75 covers Union Ministers, Article 164 covers State Ministers and Chief Ministers, and Article 239AA covers Delhi.

questions.q:
I. The Government of Union Territories (Amendment) Bill, 2025 is the second of the three Bills.
II. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirtieth Amendment) Bill, 2025 is the third of the three Bills.
III. The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2025 is the third of the three Bills.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: The Constitution Amendment Bill is the first Bill, so statement II is wrong while I and III are correct.

questions.q:
I. The JPC is expected to finalise and adopt its report.
II. The Home Minister tabled the three Bills.
III. The Prime Minister tabled the three Bills.
How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while the Prime Minister did not table the Bills according to the booklet.

questions.q: In which year was the 130th Constitution Amendment Bill introduced?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the 130th Constitution Amendment Bill was introduced in 2025.

questions.q: Which body is examining the 130th Constitution Amendment Bill? (short form)
questions.explanation: The booklet names the Joint Parliamentary Committee as the body examining the Bill.

questions.q: Which office holder tabled the three Bills? (office name)
questions.explanation: The booklet says the three Bills were tabled by the Home Minister.

questions.q: Under which Article of the Constitution are Union Ministers covered? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists Article 75 as the provision for Union Ministers.

questions.q: Under which Article are State Ministers and Chief Ministers covered? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists Article 164 as the provision for State Ministers and Chief Ministers.

questions.q: Under which Article are the Chief Minister and Ministers of Delhi covered? (number with letters)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists Article 239AA as the provision for Delhi's Chief Minister and Ministers.

questions.q: Which legislation extends the Bill's rules to Ministers of Union Territories? (full name with year)
questions.explanation: The booklet cites the Government of Union Territories Act, 1963 for Union Territory Ministers.

quizzes.title: Governance Gains and Critics' Concerns
quizzes.passage: The Bill is presented as a step toward ethical governance in public life. Supporters say it stops leaders from keeping power while facing serious charges, and that this protects public trust in institutions. It is also described as filling a gap in the law on legislators. The debate also brings in the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which sets out disqualification grounds for legislators. Supporters also point to the aim of closing constitutional gaps, which they say improves accountability in the executive. The booklet records these arguments under one heading and the concerns under another. Critics, however, have raised several concerns about how the provisions could work in practice. Their arguments focus on the position of elected state governments, on the rights of people who have been detained but not yet tried, and on the role of investigating agencies. Some critics also raise questions about the basic rights of an accused person. The concerns listed by critics are equally specific, and one of them is framed as a threat to federalism. These concerns mean the same provisions are seen in two ways, as a safeguard by some and as a risk by others. The booklet keeps both views in view, so the reader sees the reasons on each side.

questions.q: Which two agencies does the booklet say could be exploited to arrest leaders on weak charges?
questions.explanation: The booklet names the ED and CBI as agencies that could be misused to arrest leaders on weak charges.

questions.q: Under the Representation of the People Act, legislators are disqualified only after which stage of a case?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the RPA disqualifies legislators only post-conviction.

questions.q: What term does the booklet use for the anomaly that the Bill removes?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the Bill eliminates the 'governance from jail' anomaly.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Bill is said to remove the 'governance from jail' anomaly.
Reason (R): The Bill addresses interim arrests, which the Representation of the People Act does not address.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and addressing interim arrests is what removes the governance from jail anomaly.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Public Interest Foundation PIL (2018)   ->   A. Only Parliament can legislate on disqualification
II. Law Commission 170th Report   ->   B. Recommended disqualification at the framing of charges
III. Section 8(1), Representation of the People Act   ->   C. Disqualification on mere conviction for promoting enmity between groups
IV. Lily Thomas case (2013)   ->   D. Struck down Section 8(4) as invalid
questions.explanation: Each case or report is matched to the holding or recommendation the booklet attributes to it.

questions.q:
I. The Bill is said to uphold constitutional morality.
II. Critics say the Bill upholds the presumption of innocence.
III. Critics say the Bill could let the Centre destabilise opposition-led states through targeted arrests.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement II is wrong because critics say the Bill contravenes the presumption of innocence.

questions.q:
I. The Bill is said to uphold constitutional morality.
II. The Bill is said to protect public trust by acting against criminalisation of politics.
III. The Bill is said to make removal depend on conviction.
How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while the booklet says removal depends on detention rather than conviction.

questions.q: The RPA disqualifies legislators only after which stage of a criminal case? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet says the RPA disqualifies only post-conviction.

questions.q: What term does the booklet use for the anomaly the Bill removes? (three words)
questions.explanation: The booklet refers to the 'governance from jail' anomaly that the Bill eliminates.

questions.q: Which two agencies could be exploited to arrest leaders on weak charges? (acronyms)
questions.explanation: The booklet names the ED and CBI as the agencies at risk of such misuse.

questions.q: Which principle does the Bill allegedly contravene? (short phrase)
questions.explanation: Critics say removal based solely on detention contravenes the 'innocent until proven guilty' principle.

questions.q: Under the Public Interest Foundation PIL (2018), which body alone can legislate on disqualification? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet says the Supreme Court held that only Parliament can legislate on disqualification.

questions.q: Which body's 170th report recommended disqualification at the framing of charges? (name of body)
questions.explanation: The booklet cites the Law Commission's 170th Report for this recommendation.

questions.q: What principle does the Bill say it upholds? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet says the Bill upholds constitutional morality and ethical governance.

quizzes.title: How a Constitution Amendment Bill Passes
quizzes.passage: Amending the Constitution follows a formal path that the booklet traces as a flow chart. A proposal is first drafted as a Bill and then introduced in Parliament. The Bill is then put to a vote, and the voting rules are more demanding than those for ordinary legislation. The booklet explains how the votes are counted and what happens when the count is level. The booklet sets out the vote thresholds for each House in its diagram. A Bill's stages are shown in order, and each stage has its own requirement, which differs for each House. After the chambers complete their votes, the Bill moves to the next stage in the process. The sequence ends with a formal step that follows the completion of the House stages. The booklet also connects this process with other parts of the Constitution and with case law on legislators. The chart includes a box listing the provisions and legal cases that relate to the process. The booklet presents the process with simple labels, so each step can be read on its own. The flow chart's steps are numbered, so the order of the process is easy to follow. A reader can compare the stages with the list of provisions in the box to see how the process connects to the wider law.

questions.q: Which Houses must pass a Constitution amendment Bill?
options: Both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the Bill must be passed by both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.

questions.q: What happens when the votes in a House are tied?
options: The Presiding Officer of the house can cast his or her vote
The Bill is sent to a committee
questions.explanation: The booklet says the Presiding Officer of a house can cast the deciding vote in a tie.

questions.q: To whom is the passed Constitution amendment Bill presented?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the passed Bill is presented to the President.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Anti-Defection Law is among the related provisions listed for this process.
Reason (R): Articles 102 and 191 are also among the related provisions listed for this process.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but listing Articles 102 and 191 does not explain why the Anti-Defection Law is listed.

questions.q:
I. A Constitution amendment Bill can be introduced in either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha.
II. The President can refuse consent to a passed amendment Bill.
III. The President's consent is required before the Bill becomes law.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: The President is bound to give consent, so statement II is wrong while I and III are correct.

questions.q:
I. The Lily Thomas case is listed among the related matters for this process.
II. The passed Bill is presented to the Speaker of Lok Sabha before assent.
III. Articles 102 and 191 are listed among the related provisions.
How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and III are correct, while the passed Bill is presented to the President rather than the Speaker.

questions.q: After the President gives assent, the Bill becomes what?
questions.explanation: The booklet says that after assent the Bill becomes an Act.
